title: Ex-US General Calls Pakistan, Qatar 'Compromised Mediators' in Iran Talks
excerpt: Retired Gen. Jack Keane's allegation comes as Trump cancels strikes on Iran and contradictory signals emerge over whether negotiations are actually underway.
body:
• Retired Gen. Jack Keane, a Fox News strategic analyst, has accused Pakistan and Qatar of being 'compromised mediators' who favor Iran at the expense of US interests in ongoing diplomatic efforts.
  • Trump called off authorized 'massive attacks' on Iran over the weekend, citing upcoming talks — but Tehran denied any negotiations were planned or underway.
  • Qatar presented Iran with a fresh proposal on Saturday to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Iranian diplomats reportedly received positively.
  • The five-month-old US-Iran war remains unresolved, with oil prices volatile and Gulf states divided between de-escalation and hawkish approaches.

Retired US General Jack Keane has leveled a pointed accusation at Pakistan and Qatar, calling them "compromised mediators" who favor Iran at the expense of American interests in the protracted diplomatic efforts to end the five-month-old US-Iran conflict.

The allegation by Keane, a former Army Vice Chief of Staff and prominent Fox News strategic analyst, comes at a particularly fraught moment in the conflict. President Donald Trump abruptly called off what he described as authorized "massive attacks" on Iran over the weekend, saying talks were imminent — only for Tehran to flatly deny that any negotiations were underway or planned.

The Mediation Question

Pakistan and Qatar have served as the primary intermediaries between Washington and Tehran since the conflict began in late February. Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has been among the most visible diplomatic figures, claiming in June that the two sides had reached a "final, agreed upon text" — though that framework subsequently collapsed in early July.

Keane's critique reflects a broader skepticism within US national security circles about the reliability of intermediaries who maintain close ties to Tehran. "I'm highly skeptical... This is a regime for 47 years. They are pathological liars and they're cheaters. It's very difficult to take them at their word," Keane said in a Fox Business appearance.

"Pakistani mediators compromised, favour Iran at expense of US."

— Gen. Jack Keane (Ret.), Fox News Strategic Analyst

Contradictory Signals

The diplomatic confusion deepened on Monday when Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that talks "are going on right now," calling it a "last chance" for Iran to sign a deal. Hours earlier, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei had said no negotiations were taking place and no meetings were scheduled.

A senior Iranian source told Reuters that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi was on a religious pilgrimage in Iraq and would be unavailable at least until week's end. The only talks underway, Tehran said, were discussions with Oman over management of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump later escalated his rhetoric on Truth Social, calling Iran's leadership "unbelievably duplicitous" and claiming they had requested a meeting.

Gulf States Divided

Behind the diplomatic theater, Gulf states remain divided over strategy. According to the Wall Street Journal, Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump just hours before the cancelled strikes, urging dialogue and asking for clarity on US strategy. Saudi Arabia has consistently favored de-escalation.

The UAE, by contrast, has lobbied Trump to take more decisive military action, arguing that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps will not compromise until Washington escalates, senior Gulf officials told the Journal.

Qatar's mediators presented Iran with a fresh proposal on Saturday to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian diplomats reportedly reacted positively, raising hopes of a compromise on the waterway that normally carries 20% of global oil trade. However, a key sticking point remains: Iran's desire to collect fees or tolls from ships passing through the strait, which Washington has strongly opposed.

Stakes for the Diaspora

The conflict's trajectory has significant implications for the Indian diaspora. The Gulf states collectively host over eight million Indian workers and professionals, many in countries that have faced Iranian missile attacks during the war. Oil price volatility driven by the Hormuz dispute has contributed to inflationary pressures in India and raised shipping costs for trade routes critical to Indian commerce.

Oil prices fell about 5% on Monday after Trump's decision to hold off on strikes, with Brent crude futures dropping to around $83.52 a barrel — offering temporary relief but underscoring the conflict's ongoing economic ripple effects.
